newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland sees no clash between OSCE and NATO growth.
newsitem.headline: Poland sees no clash between OSCE and NATO growth.

text.p: Poland, soon to be invited to join NATO, argued at an OSCE parliamentary session in Warsaw on Saturday against suggestions by Russia and other critics that there was a clash between the developing roles of the two security bodies.
But Russian delegates sniped at plans for NATO growth, saying the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe should play the chief security role in the next century.

While stressing the OSCE's unique importance, Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski said at the start of the July 5-8 session that his countrymen placed their trust in the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.

"Nine out of 10 Poles favour joining NATO," said Kwasniewski in the Warsaw parliament, opening the annual meeting of around 300 legislators from OSCE states -- a forum for discussion in between the body's decision-making summits.
Warsaw is to be asked at a Madrid summit next week, along with Prague and Budapest which also escaped Soviet domination in 1989, to begin talks on joining the Western defence pact.
"In recent months I have heard fears the expected enlargement of NATO may weaken the OSCE," Kwasniewski said.

"I am convinced there is no contradiction between an enlarged NATO and a strengthened OSCE," he said, adding that the latter was the only body bringing together Europe, North America and the former Soviet states east of the Urals.
The Russian delegation said it would propose amendments to a document, endorsed by the OSCE's Lisbon summit in December, to strengthen the body's security model for the 21st century.
The Russian Duma's speaker, Gennady Seleznyov, said Poland's coming step towards NATO entry would change little.
"Poland will only increase its spending, because you have to be a rich country to be in NATO," he told Reuters.
But he said that if there was a move to admit Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia to NATO, Russia might revoke the founding act agreement it signed this year with the Western pact.
"We have clearly stated in Russia that if the Baltic states are taken into NATO, Russia will review the agreement which it has today with NATO, and will probably revoke it," he said.

Seleznyov said he could not understand why such states as Romania, the Czech Republic or Hungary wanted to join NATO as no one was threatening them and he dismissed arguments that NATO would confirm them in Western democratic civilisation.
"I don't think it is an entry into European civilisation to enter a military bloc," he said.
Some members of disarmament and other informal pressure groups, holding an alternative meeting alongside the OSCE session, demonstrated outside parliament against European Union and NATO enlargement.
Poland is due to take over the OSCE presidency next year.
Kwasniewski said that among the OSCE's tasks now were overcoming crises in Bosnia, Albania and Chechnya and overseeing Bosnian municipal elections in September.

In 1998 the OSCE is to replace a United Nations force in Eastern Slavonia and intensify bids to settle conflicts in Nagorno-Karabakh and Abkhazia, and it may strengthen its presence in Belarus to help develop democracy, Kwasniewski said.
Apart from the document on security in the 21st century, the OSCE parliamentary session, which was held last year in Stockholm, will also debate economic and media issues.

The OSCE, originating in the 1970s as a forum for East-West dialogue, has in recent years built a role as a monitor of democracy, human rights and arms control, helping with peacekeeping and overseeing elections.
